scripts.radio:
Good evening, and welcome back to Kenya on Record, your weekly check-in on the numbers shaping our lives.

This week, we're looking at family health. New data shows Kenya's fertility rate has dropped to 3 children per woman, down from much higher levels in past decades. Alongside this, teen pregnancy has also fallen, now standing at 11.9 percent nationally.

What does this mean for us? A lower fertility rate often points to better access to family planning, more girls staying in school longer, and improved healthcare across the country. The drop in teen pregnancy is especially encouraging — it suggests more young girls are being protected, educated, and given real choices about their futures.

But numbers on a page don't tell the whole story. In some counties, teen pregnancy remains stubbornly high, and access to reproductive health services is still uneven between urban and rural areas. So while we celebrate this national trend, we must ask: is every county, every community, feeling this progress equally?

As citizens, we have a role — to support community health workers, talk openly with our young people, and hold our leaders accountable for equal access to health services countrywide.

That's your Kenya on Record for this week. Numbers matter, but so does what we do with them.

Kwa ufupi kwa Kiswahili: Kiwango cha uzazi nchini Kenya kimeshuka hadi watoto watatu kwa kila mwanamke, na mimba za utotoni zimeshuka hadi asilimia 11.9. Hii ni ishara nzuri, lakini bado kuna haja ya kuhakikisha huduma za afya ya uzazi zinafika kila kona ya nchi.
scripts.voice_note:
Hey, hope you're doing well. Quick one for you this week from Kenya on Record.

So, new numbers are out, and they're actually pretty interesting. Kenya's fertility rate has dropped to 3 children per woman — that's down significantly from where we used to be. And get this — teen pregnancy has also fallen, now at 11.9 percent nationally.

Why does this matter? Well, it tells us families are having more say over their reproductive choices, more girls are staying in school, and maybe, just maybe, our health systems are doing something right.

But there's always a but — national averages can hide a lot. Some counties are still struggling with high teen pregnancy numbers. So the real question is, are these gains reaching everyone, or just certain areas?

Anyway, that's the data story this week. Something to think about, something to discuss with your family. Share this with someone who'd find it useful. Tutaonana next week, Kenya on Record.
scripts.sms: Usiibiwe tip: Family planning services are FREE at public health facilities. Don't pay anyone claiming it's a mandatory fee.
scripts.reels: Kenya's fertility rate has dropped to 3 children per woman. Teen pregnancy? Down to 11.9 percent. Behind these numbers — more girls staying in school, more families making informed choices, healthcare reaching further than before. But progress isn't equal everywhere. Some counties are still being left behind. This week, Kenya on Record asks: are these wins reaching every community, or just the lucky few? Numbers tell a story — it's up to us to keep it honest.
